CAPTIVE AUDIENCE MEETINGS — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jane Doe · Acme Inc.

ABOUT THIS INFORMATION SHEET
This information sheet describes California Labor Code § 1137, the "California Worker Freedom from Employer Intimidation Act," which took effect January 1, 2025. Section 1137 addresses so-called "captive audience" meetings: it restricts an employer's ability to require attendance at, or participation in, employer-sponsored meetings or communications whose purpose is to communicate the employer's opinion about religious or political matters, and it sets out the exceptions, exempt entities, and remedies the statute itself defines. This document is distinct from Acme Inc.'s existing information sheet on Labor Code §§ 1101-1106, which protects an employee's own political activities and affiliations away from work. Section 1137 instead regulates what an employer may require employees to attend or listen to at work concerning the employer's own religious or political opinions. This sheet states the text and structure of the statute. It does not describe Acme Inc.'s own meeting practices, does not determine whether any particular meeting falls within the statute's exceptions or exemptions, and does not advise Jane Doe on whether to raise a concern or take any action.

STATUTORY DEFINITIONS
Labor Code § 1137(b) defines the terms used elsewhere in the statute. "Employee" means any individual who performs services for and under the control and direction of an employer for wages or other remuneration. "Employer" is defined broadly and expressly reaches government entities. "Political matters" is defined to include not only partisan elections but also legislation, regulation, and the decision to join or support a political or labor organization. "Religious matters" is defined to include religious affiliation and practice and the decision to join or support a religious organization or association.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "“Employer” means any individual, partnership, association, corporation, or any agent, representative, designee, or person or group of persons acting directly or indirectly on behalf of or in the interest of an employer with the employer’s consent and shall include all branches of state government, or the several counties, cities and counties, and municipalities thereof, or any other political subdivision of the state, or a school district, or any special district, or any authority, commission, or board or any other agency or instrumentality thereof."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 1137(b)(2) (definition of "Employer"), Cal. Lab. Code § 1137(b)(2) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=1137)
  "“Political matters” means matters relating to elections for political office, political parties, legislation, regulation, and the decision to join or support any political party or political or labor organization."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 1137(b)(3) (definition of "Political matters"), Cal. Lab. Code § 1137(b)(3) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=1137)
  "“Religious matters” means matters relating to religious affiliation and practice and the decision to join or support any religious organization or association."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 1137(b)(4) (definition of "Religious matters"), Cal. Lab. Code § 1137(b)(4) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=1137)
  Known gap: The statute does not further define terms within these definitions, such as "control and direction" or "wages or other remuneration"; those terms carry whatever meaning they have elsewhere in the Labor Code and case law, which this sheet does not survey. The definition of "political matters" expressly includes the decision to join or support a "labor organization," meaning this section can overlap with separate labor-relations statutes not covered here.

SHORT TITLE AND EFFECTIVE DATE
The chapter containing Labor Code § 1137 is officially titled the "California Worker Freedom from Employer Intimidation Act." It was added by Statutes 2024, Chapter 670, Section 1 (Senate Bill 399), and became effective January 1, 2025.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "This chapter shall be known, and may be cited, as the “California Worker Freedom from Employer Intimidation Act.”"
  — Cal. Labor Code § 1137(a) (short title), Cal. Lab. Code § 1137(a) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=1137)
  "(Added by Stats. 2024, Ch. 670, Sec. 1. (SB 399) Effective January 1, 2025.)"
  — Cal. Labor Code § 1137, historical note (effective date), Cal. Lab. Code § 1137, Historical Note (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=1137)
  Known gap: This clause states only the statute's own title and effective date. It does not address whether any conduct that occurred before January 1, 2025 is affected, and it does not describe any local ordinance or other state's law that may independently regulate similar meetings.

CORE PROHIBITION ON MANDATORY RELIGIOUS OR POLITICAL MEETINGS
Subject to the exceptions and exemptions the statute defines, Labor Code § 1137(c) prohibits an employer from subjecting or threatening to subject an employee to discharge, discrimination, retaliation, or any other adverse action because the employee declines to attend an employer-sponsored meeting, or affirmatively declines to participate in, receive, or listen to communications with the employer, where the purpose is to communicate the employer's opinion about religious or political matters. The statute separately provides that an employee who is working at the time of such a meeting and elects not to attend continues to be paid while the meeting is held.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "shall not subject, or threaten to subject, an employee to discharge, discrimination, retaliation, or any other adverse action because the employee declines to attend an employer-sponsored meeting or affirmatively declines to participate in, receive, or listen to any communications with the employer or its agents or representatives, the purpose of which is to communicate the employer’s opinion about religious or political matters."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 1137(c) (prohibition on adverse action for declining attendance), Cal. Lab. Code § 1137(c) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=1137)
  "An employee who is working at the time of the meeting and elects not to attend a meeting described in this subdivision shall continue to be paid while the meeting is held."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 1137(c) (continued pay while meeting held), Cal. Lab. Code § 1137(c) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=1137)
  Known gap: This clause states the general rule of subdivision (c) only; it does not restate the specific exceptions in subdivision (g) or the categorical exemptions in subdivision (h), both of which limit when subdivision (c) applies and are addressed in separate clauses. The statute does not define "adverse action" for purposes of this section, and no reported California appellate decision construing Section 1137 was located in this research (the statute took effect January 1, 2025).

COMMUNICATIONS THE STATUTE DOES NOT PROHIBIT
Labor Code § 1137(g) states that the section does not prohibit an employer from communicating information the employer is legally required to communicate (limited to the extent of that legal requirement), or from communicating information necessary for employees to perform their job duties. Subdivision (g) also states the section does not prohibit an institution of higher education from meeting with employees as part of coursework, symposia, or an academic program, and does not prohibit a public entity employer from communicating information related to a public policy or a law or regulation the public entity administers.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "An employer from communicating to its employees any information that the employer is required by law to communicate, but only to the extent of that legal requirement."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 1137(g)(1) (legally required communications), Cal. Lab. Code § 1137(g)(1) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=1137)
  "An employer from communicating to its employees any information that is necessary for those employees to perform their job duties."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 1137(g)(2) (job-duty-necessary communications), Cal. Lab. Code § 1137(g)(2) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=1137)
  Known gap: This clause quotes two of the four items listed in subdivision (g); the higher-education and public-entity-policy items are stated in summary rather than quoted verbatim. The statute does not define how much communication falls within "the extent of that legal requirement" or what makes information "necessary" to job duties, so where a specific communication falls on either side of that line is not addressed by the statutory text itself.

ENTITIES AND ACTIVITIES THE STATUTE DOES NOT COVER
Labor Code § 1137(h) lists six categories to which the section does not apply at all, including: certain religious corporations, entities, associations, educational institutions, or societies (with respect to speech on religious matters to employees connected with their religious activities, as described in subdivision (h)(1)); a political organization or party requiring attendance at a meeting to communicate the organization's own political tenets or purposes; an educational institution requiring attendance at lectures that are part of regular coursework; a nonprofit tax-exempt training program requiring attendance related to its mission; an employer requiring training to comply with legal obligations, including civil rights and occupational safety and health laws; and a public employer holding a statutorily defined new employee orientation, or certain other statutorily defined orientations.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "A political organization or party requiring its employees to attend an employer-sponsored meeting or to participate in any communications with the employer or its agents or representatives, the purpose of which is to communicate the employer’s political tenets or purposes."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 1137(h)(2) (political organization exemption), Cal. Lab. Code § 1137(h)(2) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=1137)
  "An employer requiring employees to undergo training to comply with the employer’s legal obligations, including obligations under civil rights laws and occupational safety and health laws."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 1137(h)(5) (legal-compliance training exemption), Cal. Lab. Code § 1137(h)(5) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=1137)
  Known gap: The religious-corporation exemption in subdivision (h)(1) cross-references Title VII of the federal Civil Rights Act and several California Government Code and Labor Code provisions defining which employers and what conduct qualify; this clause summarizes rather than quotes that cross-referenced exemption, and this research did not independently verify the current text of those cross-referenced provisions. Determining whether a specific entity or meeting fits within any of the six listed exemptions requires matching its facts against the statute's own wording, which this sheet does not do.

ENFORCEMENT AND REMEDIES
Labor Code § 1137 provides more than one enforcement path. Under subdivision (d), an employer who violates the section is subject to a civil penalty of five hundred dollars ($500) per employee for each violation, in addition to any other remedy. Under subdivision (e), the Labor Commissioner may enforce the section, including investigating an alleged violation, ordering temporary relief, and issuing a citation, using the procedures set out in Labor Code §§ 98.3, 98.7, 98.74, or 1197.1. Under subdivision (f), as an alternative to Labor Commissioner enforcement, an employee who has suffered a violation of subdivision (c) may instead bring a civil action for damages, including punitive damages, and may petition the superior court for temporary or preliminary injunctive relief.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "an employer who violates this section shall be subject to a civil penalty of five hundred dollars ($500) per employee for each violation."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 1137(d) (civil penalty), Cal. Lab. Code § 1137(d) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=1137)
  "The Labor Commissioner may enforce this section, including investigating an alleged violation, and ordering appropriate temporary relief to mitigate a violation or maintain the status quo pending the completion of a full investigation or hearing through the procedures set forth in Section 98.3, 98.7, 98.74, or 1197.1, including issuing a citation against an employer who violates this section and filing a civil action."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 1137(e) (Labor Commissioner enforcement), Cal. Lab. Code § 1137(e) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=1137)
  "any employee who has suffered a violation of subdivision (c) may bring a civil action in a court of competent jurisdiction for damages caused by that adverse action, including punitive damages."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 1137(f)(1) (private civil action), Cal. Lab. Code § 1137(f)(1) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=1137)
  Known gap: This clause describes the remedies subdivision (d), (e), and (f) make available; it does not reproduce the full text of the cross-referenced enforcement procedures in Labor Code §§ 98.3, 98.7, 98.74, or 1197.1, which were not independently fetched and verified in this research. A CourtListener case-law search for judicial decisions applying Section 1137 returned a rate-limit error (HTTP 429, quota exhausted) before any results could be reviewed, so this sheet cannot state whether courts have yet interpreted these remedies; given the statute's January 1, 2025 effective date, reported appellate decisions may not yet exist regardless.

ACKNOWLEDGMENT OF RECEIPT
By signing below, Jane Doe acknowledges receiving this information sheet describing California Labor Code § 1137, the California Worker Freedom from Employer Intimidation Act, from Acme Inc. This acknowledgment confirms only that the information sheet was received and reviewed. It is not a statement about whether any meeting at Acme Inc. does or does not fall within the statute, and it does not waive any right or remedy the statute provides.

Employee signature: ______________________________

Employee name: Jane Doe

Date signed: January 1, 2026
